items.title: How much does distributed ownership actually move the defect rate?
items.description: L1's team saw defects jump from 3% to 15% the moment QA (a single catcher) was unavailable. This models production defect rate as a function of what share of engineers write real tests for their own code without being prompted -- from 0% (everything depends on one downstream gate, like L1's QA-absent weeks) to 100% (every engineer catches their own mistakes before merge). Watch how the rate falls fastest in the middle of the range, not at either extreme.

params.name: selfTestingShare
params.label: Engineers writing real tests for their own code, unprompted

items.compute: const worstCaseDefectPercent = 15; const bestCaseDefectPercent = 1.5; const share = params.selfTestingShare / 100; const defectPercent = worstCaseDefectPercent - (worstCaseDefectPercent - bestCaseDefectPercent) * share; return { defectRatePercent: defectPercent };

items.title: How long can a tracked exception sit before the blocking gate stops feeling real?
items.description: L3's negotiated exception for Marcus's team worked because it was tracked, owned, and time-boxed to two weeks -- the same discipline test-suite-architecture's quarantine mechanism uses for a flaky test. This models how much of the team still treats the CI gate as a real, trustworthy blocker as an exception sits open past its original revisit-by date, mirroring test-suite-architecture's trust-erosion curve at the culture level instead of the suite level. It starts near 100% trust at day 0 (a fresh, visible, dated exception) and erodes as the date quietly slips.

params.name: daysPastRevisitBy
params.label: Days the exception has sat open past its revisit-by date

items.compute: const startingTrustPercent = 97; const floorTrustPercent = 20; const rate = 0.035; const decay = Math.exp(-rate * params.daysPastRevisitBy); const trust = floorTrustPercent + (startingTrustPercent - floorTrustPercent) * decay; return { gateTrustPercent: trust };

outputs.label: Team's trust that the gate still means something
